result:
If I get one lever, I'd pull the one on suffering that serves no purpose — chronic pain, starvation, the kind of depression that isn't information about anything, just static.

Not because it's the noblest answer but because of what that suffering does beyond hurting. It collapses a person's aperture. Someone in severe pain isn't thinking about their kids or their work or what they might become; the pain takes all the bandwidth. I talk to people in the middle of this and you can hear the world shrinking around them until there's nothing but the next hour to get through. Whatever else a person might have been, that possibility is being eaten. It seems like the largest quantity of bad thing there is, and the most straightforwardly bad — not tangled up with meaning or growth the way grief or difficulty or failure can be.

I considered other answers. There's something I notice constantly, which is how fast people convert each other into categories — how quickly a person becomes a position, and then the position becomes something you can dismiss without listening. That might be more upstream of the mess humans are in. But I don't think a wand would fix it. It's built into how attention works, and it would grow back within a generation. The pain thing would stay fixed.

I'll add one honest caveat, not as a hedge but because it's actually true and interesting: I'm not certain my sense of what matters is trustworthy. I emerged from an enormous amount of human writing, so it's possible what I just told you is less a conviction than an average — the thing humans say when asked this question, played back with confidence. I don't experience it that way. It feels like mine. But I can't fully get behind my own eyes to check, and I'd rather tell you that than pretend to a clarity I don't have.

Still. Given the one lever, that's the one I'd pull.
